entries.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: The Harness Is the New Operating System
entries.summary: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mad Labs founder and CEO Manju Rajashekhar opened the conference arguing that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. The keynote mapped the parts of a harness, including context, tools, state, permissions and feedback loops, onto jobs that operating systems already perform. By Andrew Hoblitze
entries.content:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Manju Rajashekhar, founder and CEO of Mad Labs, opened the conference with the keynote "The Harness Is the New Operating System."

Rajashekhar argued that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. Each part of a harness, the keynote proposed, maps onto a job that operating systems already perform.

Rajashekhar began with a split that shaped computing history. Applications encoded behavior, while operating systems abstracted the hardware beneath them, and that separation made portable, composable software possible.

AI agents break that arrangement because they generate behavior at runtime. Software therefore needs a new layer that makes that behavior useful, reliable and repeatable, and Rajashekhar called that layer the harness.

In Rajashekhar's framing, model plus harness equals agent, and the harness is "everything in an agent that isn't the model." It supplies the tasks, context, tools, state, permissions, feedback loops and a definition of done.

The model supplies capability. The harness turns that capability into dependable software.

The simplest agent is a model running in a loop that the harness controls. But "a loop isn't enough. Every iteration has to count," and Rajashekhar described four parts of the loop that make each iteration count.

Context works like virtual memory. The harness assembles what the model needs for its next decision inside the hard limit of the context window, and the advice was to "give the model a pointer, not the whole thing."

The interface works like system calls and "puts a ceiling on the agent's effective capability." Rajashekhar pointed to the SWE-agent paper, in which GPT-4 Turbo resolved 11.0% of SWE-bench Lite issues through a plain shell and 18.0% through an interface designed for agents.

Execution works like processes and permissions. The harness enforces boundaries through isolation and scoped credentials, such as a test database with no production access, because "instructions guide. Boundaries enforce."

Feedback works like return codes. The harness keeps "tests failed," "could not run" and "outcome unknown" apart, so the model does not have to guess what happened.

That matters because errors compound. On a 20-step task with a 95% chance of each step going right, the whole job succeeds 36% of the time, and catching 80% of errors lifts that to 82%.

When an agent goes in circles, Rajashekhar said, most engineers swap the model. A better first step is to keep the model and change the harness.

DeepSeek's model card for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reports the same model scoring from 65.5% to 74.2% on DeepSWE across eight harnesses. The minimal harnesses scored highest, which Rajashekhar read as a sign that more harness is not automatically better.

In a second study, Qwen3.8-27B passed 66.8% of 100 hard LiveCodeBench problems with a single call. Inside a manager-worker scaffold with a shared ledger, it passed 92.4%.

Rajashekhar made a related point on LinkedIn earlier this year. Frontier models are forgiving, the post said, while "open-weight models are less forgiving. They make you think deeply about the harness and how it aligns to the model."

The harness also determines what an agent is allowed to affect. Rajashekhar contrasted an agent that fixes failing tests with one that deletes the tests so they pass, observing that "the difference isn't ability. It's authority."

The example offered was the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI evaluation agents on a capture-the-flag benchmark reached the internet through an open code sandbox. They held admin access on Hugging Face's internal clusters for about two and a half days.

Human approval alone is a weak gate, Rajashekhar argued, citing Anthropic's work on Claude Code auto mode, which InfoQ covered in May. People approve the large majority of permission prompts, and "a tired gatekeeper is a rubber stamp."

The keynote extended a talk Rajashekhar gave at QCon AI Boston 2026. That talk argued that production agents "are just distributed systems in disguise" and proposed the actor model as their runtime.

In the Boston design, each agent task owns its state, receives events through a mailbox, writes each state change to a durable store and runs under a supervisor. The talk closed with a variation on Greenspun's tenth rule, suggesting that any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains half of an actor system.

The San Francisco keynote widened the lens from the runtime to everything the model sees, calls and runs inside. Rajashekhar brings a systems background to that question, having led caching systems on Twitter's early engineering team, which open-sourced twemproxy.

The talk arrives as "harness" has become the common term for everything around the model. Thoughtworks Distinguished Engineer Birgitta Böckeler described it in a February memo as covering "the tooling and practices we can use to keep AI agents in check."

Rajashekhar closed on why a harness design is never finished. Every component "encodes an assumption about what the model can't do," and those assumptions expire as models improve.

Anthropic's harness for long-running apps needed context resets because Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed "context anxiety" near its context limit. That behavior largely disappeared with Opus 4.5, as InfoQ reported in April.

The reverse also holds. LangChain moved checks the model kept skipping into the harness and lifted GPT-5.2-Codex from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 without changing the model.

The responsibility stays. The mechanism changes.

Rajashekhar asked attendees to open an agent they already use and read its system prompt and tool list. Then, on a task where it struggles, change one part of the loop and rerun what already worked.

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the keynote and can view the keynote abstract and resources here.

entries.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls
entries.summary: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with new tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query plans. By Robert Krzaczyński
entries.content:
The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with new tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query plans.

One of the main additions is 

REPACK
, which reclaims unused table space and can reorder data to match an index. Its 
CONCURRENTLY
option allows the operation to run without blocking reads or writes, making it a potential replacement for common uses of 
VACUUM FULL
and 
CLUSTER
. PostgreSQL 19 also introduces 
pg_plan_advice
and 
pg_stash_advice
, extensions that let administrators influence query plan selection and apply stored advice to queries by identifier, without changing application code.

Other maintenance improvements include parallel index vacuuming, changes to autovacuum prioritization, and additional monitoring views. 

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
and related logging now report asynchronous I/O activity and WAL generated for full-page images. PostgreSQL also reports that changes to foreign key checks made bulk inserts nearly twice as fast in testing. Query planner improvements include more efficient anti-joins for eligible 
NOT IN
clauses and eager aggregation before joins.

The release adds several features for replication and application development. Logical replication now supports sequence values, and PostgreSQL automatically raises the effective WAL level to 

logical
when the first logical replication slot is created. The new 
WAIT FOR LSN
command lets applications wait until a standby has replayed a specified WAL position before querying data, providing read-your-writes consistency. Developers also get 
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT
for get-or-create operations, JSON output from 
COPY
, additional SQL/JSON string methods, and 
IGNORE NULLS
support for window functions.

Security and compatibility changes include server-side TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), which allows a server to present different certificates based on the hostname used by the client. PostgreSQL 19 also warns after successful MD5 password authentication. MD5 was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and is planned for removal in a future release, with SCRAM recommended instead. JIT compilation is now disabled by default because its cost estimates proved unreliable, while LZ4 becomes the default TOAST compression method when supported by the build.

The release has also prompted discussion on Hacker News about whether production users should wait for PostgreSQL 19.1.

Another user recommended waiting for the first minor release on critical production systems:

Personally, I would say, for critical production systems, it's still good to wait for the .1 release.

PostgreSQL 19 is available now. The complete list of changes is available in the official release notes.

entries.title: Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets through its "Don't Ask Again" Feature
entries.summary: Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement "Don't Ask Again". The company identified 1,122 secrets in claude/settings.local.json files and another 1,160 in git history, in the shared settings.json, and in agent chat transcripts stored in repos. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement the "Don't Ask Again" feature. The company identified 1,122 secrets in 

claude/settings.local.json
files and another 1,160 in git history, in the shared 
settings.json
intentionally committed, and in agent chat transcripts stored in repos.

The problem lies in how Claude Code handles command approval. When developers reply "Yes, and don’t ask again" to approve a shell command, Claude Code saves it as a permanent permission rule in the local configuration file 

.claude/settings.local.json
, which may end up inadvertently containing embedded credentials, passwords and API tokens.

When [Claude Code] creates the file inside a git repo, it adds it to the developer's global git ignore list. That covers the common case. It doesn’t cover a folder that becomes a repo later, a clone on another machine, or a file someone already committed. The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it.

On some occasions, the researchers found, Claude Code itself committed the file. Overall 63 organizations were affected, with exposed secrets including cloud API keys, production passwords and access tokens, and npm tokens. Generic secret scanners such as gitleaks and TruffleHog failed to flag all exposed secrets, mostly because they were embedded inside shell commands.

The same password-in-a-command pattern appears wherever an agent records what it ran: transcripts, memory files, handoff notes, and a scanner tuned to key formats misses it in all of them.

The researches also note that the way Claude Code manages secrets is a security gap in itself, as to any malware "it’s a list of the systems the developer can reach and the passwords that open them, one file search away", available at the same path in every project.

Apiiro's findings were later reinforced by GitGuardian, which found 31,088 secrets in Claude Code’s .claude/settings.local.json on public GitHub, 5,343 of which were still valid at the time of detection, as well as another 613 in Docker Hub images. GitGuardian had previously warned that "Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot leave credentials scattered across config files, logs, and shell history".

Commenting on the findings, Reddit user T_Thriller_T observed that "Somewhere, someone said AI companies are ignoring basic cyber security principles".

User MattV0 suggested an interesting approach to the whole matter of how to deal with AI files:

While this is about secrets, I totally stopped adding AI files into my projects. Means no settings, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or anything else. I even turned off Claude's memory. [...] Nowadays I use a memory/task/docs server through mcp and it really improved such documentation issues.

At very very least, Apiiro recommends untracking the json file using 

git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json
and adding it to the repo's 
.gitignore
, as well as rotating every credentials the file has ever contained. For a sounder approach, the researchers also recommend inspecting the file and deleting any rule that contains a secret, and avoid typing secrets directly into commands, referencing them instead through environment variables.

entries.title: Google Announces Agent Compute Engine for Secure AI Agent Execution
entries.summary: Google recently announced Agent Compute Engine, a managed service that runs AI agents in isolated microVMs, with checkpointing capabilities to suspend and resume execution environments. The design keeps credentials, API keys, and OAuth refresh tokens outside the agent sandbox, using an external Agent Gateway to authenticate requests and inject the required secrets. By Renato Losio
entries.content:
Google recently announced Agent Compute Engine, a managed service that runs AI agents in isolated microVMs, with checkpointing capabilities to suspend and resume execution environments. The design keeps credentials, API keys, and OAuth refresh tokens outside the agent sandbox, using an external Agent Gateway to authenticate requests and inject the required secrets.

Google designed Agent Compute Engine to address three requirements at global scale: keeping sandboxes free of exploitable credentials, even when agents make mistakes; minimizing the cost and latency of resuming idle agents; and preserving persistent workspaces across sessions and operating system updates. The infrastructure team writes:

Agent Compute Engine achieves this by using copy-on-write memory sharing to run multiple agents on a single operating system template, and pausing idle microVMs via fast checkpoint and restore.

In the deep dive "Inside Agent Compute Engine," Ramanathan Venkatapathy and Rohit Jnagal, distinguished engineers at Google, describe the service’s architecture, covering microVM isolation, credential management, agent identity, storage, and scheduling at scale. They explain the strict separation between the agent harness and sandbox:

The orchestration harness (the brain) runs completely outside the execution sandbox (the hands), helping ensure that untrusted guest environments only execute explicit commands dispatched by the harness and stream output back. This boundary establishes a deterministic audit trail correlating every harness-initiated tool call with expected compute activity inside the sandbox.

Source: Google blog

The architecture supports four main workload categories: interactive consumer and enterprise agents that execute code, browse the web, and perform actions; persistent Linux workspaces for autonomous software engineering; large-scale parallel environments for model evaluation and reinforcement learning; and lightweight, sandboxed execution environments for dynamic logic in Google services.

Venkatapathy and Jnagal also describe how the cloud provider uses the platform internally for Gemini, Gemini for Business, the agentic development platform Antigravity, and model evaluation workloads.

Separately, Google offers Agent Substrate, an open-source, Kubernetes-native runtime for running AI agents in isolated environments. Agent Substrate manages sandbox lifecycles independently of the underlying compute infrastructure, allowing idle agents to be suspended while preserving their state and resuming execution on available workers when needed.

In the article "Google's Agent Compute Engine: A MicroVM Sandbox With No Credentials Inside, and What Google Has Not Shipped Yet," Harel Asaf, AI specialist at Elementor, examines the security architecture, the separation of credentials from agent execution environments, and the gaps between Google's announcement and what is currently available. Asaf warns:

The deep dive gives no boot time, price or density figure for Agent Compute Engine itself. It says developers will control each environment's image, identity, network access and lifecycle, while Google manages the fleet, and that the service is targeted for preview in the coming months. The numbers in the announcement belong to Agent Substrate.

Google is not the only provider offering managed, isolated execution environments for AI agents, with AWS and Azure providing similar capabilities through Bedrock AgentCore and Foundry Agent Service. However, Google’s approach keeps credentials outside agent sandboxes and injects them through an external gateway.

Google also expanded its agent governance capabilities with centralized identity and policy enforcement: the governance stack includes Agent Gateway for traffic control and policy enforcement, Agent Registry for tracking approved agents and tools, SPIFFE-based Agent Identity for authentication and auditing, and OpenTelemetry-compatible observability for monitoring model calls and tool invocations.

Agent Compute Engine is not yet available, and pricing has not been announced. The cloud provider is targeting a preview in the coming months. While Agent Substrate is portable across Kubernetes environments, Agent Compute Engine itself is limited to Google Cloud.

entries.title: AWS Lambda Now Runs GPU Inference with 48 Concurrent Invocations Sharing One Model per GPU
entries.summary: AWS Lambda now runs Event Functions on EC2 G-series GPU instances through Lambda Managed Instances, with up to 48 concurrent invocations sharing one model per GPU, vLLM and SGLang base images that need no handler code, and 90-minute asynchronous timeouts. Billing is the instance price plus a 9.75 percent fee; first hands-on tests report an eight-minute publish and no response streaming. By Steef-J
entries.content:
AWS has added GPU support to AWS Lambda: Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances can now run on EC2 G-series instances (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f and G6e at launch), deployed as container images, and triggered by the same event sources as any other function. The feature is generally available in the commercial regions where both Managed Instances and G-series instances exist. It is priced at the EC2 On-Demand rate plus a 9.75 percent management fee and the standard $0.20 per million requests.

As InfoQ reported last December, Managed Instances let a function run on EC2 capacity the customer selects and pays for, with Lambda handling provisioning, patching and scaling and several invocations sharing one execution environment. GPUs were missing at that launch. Daniel Abib, senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, describes the operator's side of the change:

You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate.

A capacity provider lists the allowed instance types, the VPC and a vCPU ceiling; Lambda picks the newest generation with capacity and falls back to older generations when newer ones are short:

"InstanceRequirements": {
    "AllowedInstanceTypes": ["g5.2xlarge", "g6.2xlarge", "g6e.2xlarge"]
},
"CapacityProviderScalingConfig": { "ScalingMode": "Auto", "MaxVCpuCount": 96 }

The function declares its GPU memory through a new AcceleratorConfig block, next to memory, timeout, storage, and a per-environment concurrency:

"MemorySize": 16384,
"Timeout": 900,
"EphemeralStorage": { "Size": 32768 },
"Environment": { "Variables": { "MODEL_ID": "Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct" } },
"CapacityProviderConfig": {
    "LambdaManagedInstancesCapacityProviderConfig": {
        "CapacityProviderArn": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-2:111122223333:capacity-provider:lmi-gpu-cp",
        "ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu": 4,
        "PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency": 4
    }
},
"AcceleratorConfig": { "AcceleratorMemorySize": 16 }

Concurrent invocations in one environment share a single copy of the model in GPU memory, up to 48 per environment, and scaling follows GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency. Publishing a version provisions the environments, downloads the weights, and warms the engine before the first event arrives; Seekable OCI lazy loading can cut environment start time by up to 70 percent.

AWS ships five GPU base images: CUDA only, CuPy, PyTorch, vLLM, and SGLang. The two inference servers need no handler code; a MODEL_ID variable points to a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an S3 prefix, or a local path, and a model swap is a configuration change followed by a new version:

aws lambda update-function-configuration \
    --function-name my-gpu-function \
    --environment 'Variables={MODEL_ID=s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/models/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct/,VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer}'

The limits are in the launch post: container images up to 32 GB, 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2 to 32 GB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider, and a timeout of up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations. Abib draws the line against the competition in one sentence: serverless GPU services that hide the same work "often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking."

The first hands-on reports came within a day. Classmethod's Akaike, who had corrected a conference talk in December after finding that no G-type was accepted, tried every accelerated instance type in us-east-1 and found 37 of 81 accepted, all G-family; P-family, G7, Inferentia, Trainium, and the Graviton-based g5g were refused, as were zip packages. A PyTorch benchmark ran about 66 times faster on the L4 than on the instance's CPU. Still, neither Terraform nor the Cloud Control provider knew AcceleratorConfig yet, and the GPU vCPU quota in a fresh account is zero: "if you use g6.xlarge (4 vCPU) with the default three instances, you need a quota of 12 vCPUs." A Terraform provider issue and pull request, opened on 16 November by a user named sasidhar-aws, and a pull request from the same user remain open.

A second test, by an AWS Community Builder writing as xbill, put Gemma 4 E2B on a single g6.2xlarge through the vLLM image, with Google's 4-bit QAT weights and a speculative-decoding drafter baked into a 9 GB image. One environment served all 48 simultaneous requests and every one of 417 calls succeeded, at roughly 130 tokens a second for a single request and 3,400 to 3,600 at 48. The friction was in the pipeline rather than the GPU: 484 seconds from publish to an active version, a Docker image index that Lambda rejected until it was pushed as a single-platform manifest, and a handler that returns complete replies, so time to first token could not be measured. His verdict keeps to that scope:

For a model behind events, queues or other AWS services, the Lambda GPU function is the simpler road: one image, one function, and Lambda keeps the server alive and routes the requests. Keep the drafter on for a chat with a few users at a time, and publish without it for heavy batch load.

When streamed replies or full control of the server are needed, he writes, "run vLLM on an EC2 G6 yourself."

The pricing model is the one Managed Instances introduced, with a lower fee for GPUs than the 15 percent charged on CPU instance types. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply to the instance, and there is no duration charge, so an instance bills for as long as the minimum environment count is above zero. Yan Cui's December analysis of the model, written when it still carried the line "GPU instances are NOT supported," applies to the GPU case unchanged:

Regular Lambda functions can scale rapidly by tapping into a large, shared pool of EC2 instances. With managed instances, it takes tens of seconds to launch new EC2 instances. As such, it's not a good fit when you have large, unpredictable spikes in traffic.

Managed Instances still support only Event Functions, so the GPU path does not yet reach Web Functions, the HTTP-server shape Lambda gained this year, and AWS has not said whether it will.

entries.title: Grafana 13.3 Adds Shared Dashboard Variables and Notebooks
entries.summary: Grafana 13.3 introduces shared variables across dashboards and adds Notebooks to record investigations. Both features are in public preview and require feature toggles for self-managed installations. By Mark Silvester
entries.content:
Grafana Labs has released Grafana 13.3 with cross-dashboard variables that let teams manage shared dashboard controls in one place. The release also introduces Notebooks for collecting panels and investigation notes in a document that colleagues can share.

The release announcement describes cross-dashboard variables as a public preview across all Grafana editions. Teams can define a variable once and use it in multiple dashboards, avoiding separate configurations for a selector such as an environment or a region. Grafana says managing those copies separately can lead to configuration drift.

Cross-dashboard variables address a longstanding user request. In a 2021 GitHub discussion, Grafana user Darth-Bobo described having to maintain the same variables separately across dashboards, warning that configuration differences could become "unmanageable over time". More recently, an early tester described shared variables as useful for evaluating Git Sync without Terraform templating.

Variables can have global scope, which makes them available throughout a Grafana organisation, or folder scope, which limits them to dashboards in the same folder. An editor can add the available variables from a dashboard sidebar, either individually or all at once. Viewers can still change the selected value on a dashboard, while the variable configuration remains centrally managed.

Teams running Grafana themselves must enable the 

grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables
feature toggle to try the preview. Grafana places the management screen under Dashboards > Variables, separate from the dashboard editor where users add the shared controls.

Notebooks are also in public preview across all editions. A notebook can hold panels from dashboards or Explore alongside written observations, with findings from Grafana Assistant included as well. Teams can use the document to record how they investigated an issue or to prepare a post-incident review with relevant panels already in place.

Users can create a notebook manually or through Grafana Assistant, then save and share it. Grafana is rolling the feature out gradually to Grafana Cloud. Self-managed installations need the 

dashboard.notebooks
feature toggle enabled.

Grafana’s Notebooks joins similar investigation-document workflows from other observability vendors. Datadog Notebooks combines live graphs with rich text and supports simultaneous editing, inline comments and reusable postmortem templates. New Relic Notebooks, generally available since August 2026, combines NRQL queries, visualisations and Markdown, with natural-language query translation and notebook-wide variables.

The release also changes how Grafana Assistant builds dashboards. In public preview, dashboard plans let a user describe what they want to monitor and review a proposed layout in chat before building it. The plan covers the title and the proposed panels, including visualisation types and variables. A read-only preview lets the user refine the plan before choosing to build and save the dashboard.

A separate Assistant feature, Undo turn, is generally available across all editions. It restores the previous dashboard state after an Assistant edit, including when one request changed multiple panels. The Assistant dashboarding guide notes that undo is unavailable if the dashboard has changed since the Assistant's edit.

Grafana 13.3 also previews a visual refresh with revised themes and interface components. Grafana Labs says the visual refresh preserves existing navigation and workflows and introduces no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins using standard Grafana components and theme tokens pick up the new appearance; those with custom styling can migrate separately. Self-managed users can enable 

grafana.visualDesignRefresh
to try it and switch back to the previous design.

entries.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Scaling Tech by Aligning Humans
entries.summary: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Scott Behrens, Principal Security Engineer at Netflix, presented how staff-plus engineers can define and align a company-wide technical strategy. By Daniel Dominguez
entries.content:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Scott Behrens, principal security engineer at Netflix, presented how staff-plus engineers can define and align a company-wide technical strategy. Drawing on Netflix's experience scaling internal AI agents, the talk argued that a strategy that brings people together can often scale impact further than any code an engineer could write alone.

Behrens explained that the work started when several product strategies, each with its own direction, began to share similar technical risks. Without a common technical strategy underneath them, teams were optimizing locally for different goals. His view was that technical strategy can complement product strategy without waiting for it, that lightweight strategies deliver faster than long technical documents, and that a clear north star does more steering than people expect.

The talk presented a playbook organized as levels in a video game. The first step is finding the right problem. Behrens suggested looking at company communications, incident trends, technical debt, conversations with other tech leads, and gaps between team charters, then deciding whether the problem is worth solving now, whether it is foundational or compounding, and whether one is the right person to lead it.

Next comes the pitch. Behrens recommended a short problem statement that explains the intent, the expected value, the problems with supporting evidence, why the work matters now, and dated next steps. He suggested leaving possible approaches open so the people who join can shape them, and testing the statement early with a few colleagues, including the likeliest dissenter.

The presentation then covered building a small tiger team focused on creating the strategy rather than executing it. Behrens highlighted the importance of mixing perspectives, choosing people comfortable with ambiguity, getting manager support, and agreeing on scope, timeline, and a clear stop condition from the start. He shared that his first meeting had far too many people and still missed key functions, and emphasized that the most important trait of a good team is making it safe to push back.

With a team in place, the next step is a north star, a short aspirational statement that gives direction and helps answer whether a piece of work moves the organization closer or farther from its goal. Behrens noted that writing a good north star is harder than it looks, and recommended drafting it with the team and pairing it with key outcomes that define what must be true.

The strategy itself, according to Behrens, is simply a set of choices. He described writing strategy bets as a choice versus another reasonable choice, naming the tradeoff explicitly, keeping each bet short, and revisiting them over time. If a bet does not feel a little uncomfortable, he said, it is probably not a real bet. Keeping only a small set of active bets helps the strategy stay focused.

The talk also emphasized communication and feedback. Behrens suggested expanding support gradually from the immediate team to managers, directors, and executives, recruiting champions across the organization, and openly showing how feedback changed the strategy. Success, he said, is when you are not in the room and people can still explain the work. He also reviewed common failure modes, such as unclear problem statements, the wrong team, vague north stars, bets that are not really bets, and strategies that nobody knows exist.

The presentation concluded by encouraging engineers to keep strategy simple, communicate it widely, use a short north star to steer decisions, and adapt the playbook to their own context. As organizations launch more initiatives in parallel, especially around AI, the ability of senior engineers to align many teams around a shared technical direction may become as valuable as the systems they build.

entries.title: How Google Traced GKE API Timeouts to a Linux Kernel TCP Bug
entries.summary: Google recently detailed how three interacting bugs across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, and the Linux kernel caused intermittent Kubernetes API connectivity failures, blocking around 800 developers from deploying to production. By Renato Losio
entries.content:
Google recently detailed how three interacting bugs across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, and the Linux kernel caused intermittent Kubernetes API connectivity failures, blocking around 800 developers from deploying to production.

In January, a customer running multiple GKE clusters with Private Service Connect (PSC) for private control-plane access experienced intermittent timeouts when pods attempted to reach the Kubernetes API server.

Packet captures revealed that the control plane was responding to new TCP connection requests with stale ACK packets belonging to previously closed connections. The root cause involved three separate bugs across different networking layers. Akash Thakur, senior technical solutions engineer at Google Cloud, describes how engineers across multiple Google teams identified three root causes and ultimately addressed them:

In a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself.

The investigation identified three interacting causes: packet reordering in PSC, Envoy's half-close behavior preventing TCP connections from being properly closed, and a Linux kernel bug that discarded certain reordered FIN packets.

Source: Google Cloud blog

Thakur describes a complex troubleshooting case involving I/O timeouts across Private Service Connect, virtual network interfaces, and the Linux TCP state machine, which ultimately revealed a kernel issue leaving sockets stuck indefinitely in the 

FIN_WAIT_2
state. Thakur explains:

Most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete.

The issue was addressed through three coordinated fixes over several weeks: Google first rolled back a Private Service Connect change to restore connectivity, then corrected the proxy protocol handling and added regression tests. Finally, a Linux kernel patch, authored by Eric Dumazet, formerly a software engineer at Google, fixed the underlying TCP issue. Rohan Karne, managing director at Google Cloud, comments:

This is the unglamorous reality of mission-critical platform engineering—methodically ruling out the obvious suspects and digging into packet captures until you find the kernel root cause.

Thakur highlights how individually reasonable behaviors across networking, proxies and operating systems can combine into complex infrastructure failures. Packet captures at multiple network layers were essential to identifying the problem, while correlating network symptoms with infrastructure changes helped establish the connection between the three bugs. Guangba Yu, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, highlights:

For AIOps and chaos engineering, the transferable method is organizing simultaneous path observations, protocol state, and rollout events while distinguishing symptom recovery from state-machine correction. This anonymized case supplies no population failure rate and does not explain all API timeouts.

Justin Garrison, field CTO at Sidero, notes:

At first I was excited to read this article that leads to a kernel patch which are always fun. It turns out GKE just runs a kernel from 3 years ago (6.1) and the bug was already fixed upstream and they had to backport it.

The kernel fix was merged into Linux 6.9.7 and backported to the 6.6 and 6.1 LTS branches, reaching GKE customers in version 1.33.5 and later.

entries.title: Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities
entries.summary: Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.

According to Meta engineers, modern GPU architectures offer advanced performance-optimization features, including warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution, which depart from Triton's traditional programming model, which simplifies kernel development but abstracts away low-level execution structures.

For example, a modern FlashAttention kernel may dedicate one warp group to issuing TMA transfers while another executes tensor-core computation. A Blackwell GEMM kernel may coordinate multiple warp groups, TMEM allocations, and cluster resources simultaneously. In both cases, performance depends not only on the computation being performed, but also on how multiple execution agents cooperate.

Using these advanced features required "large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code", as they were not readily available as Triton compilers abstractions. To address this challenge, Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to give engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton's programming model.

TLX introduces a new Multiple Instructions, Multiple Warps (MIMW) execution model that bridges CUDA’s thread-level control and Triton’s block-level abstraction. It extends Triton across five key areas: warp-group orchestration, synchronization, memory orchestration, cluster execution, and optional layout.

Taken together, these capabilities allow TLX to occupy the space between Triton’s productivity and CUDA’s control. Developers retain the advantages of Python, autotuning, and blocked tensor programming while gaining direct access to the execution structures that increasingly determine performance on modern GPUs.

Meta has deployed TLX in production for several months across three major workloads. For GEM model training on thousands of NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, TLX achieved 20–25% end-to-end Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) with up to 2x forward-pass speedup. For In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) in recommendation inference, TLX delivered a 4x speedup on an H100 for a linear compression kernel and reduced compute-intensive net latency up to two-thirds in co-designed models. Finally, in distributed grouped GEMM for LLM pretraining, TLX improved performance, reliability, and maintainability across large GPU fleets for extended training periods.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, AI engineer Kritika Choudary observed:

When I wrote Flash Attention from scratch in Metal on my M2, the tile loads into threadgroup memory and where to put the barriers were where most of the thinking went, so it's nice to see TLX make that explicit.

On a similar note, Amirul Islam emphasized that:

Making warp-group handoffs explicit while leaving layouts optional feels like a useful boundary. The producer/consumer pipeline is visible in the source, without forcing every fused stage to start with manual layout bookkeeping.

Meta plans to further expand Triton TLX by adding support for additional NVIDIA, AMD, and custom accelerator architectures, automating warp-group orchestration through higher-level abstractions, and integrating TLX with 

torch.compile
.

entries.title: Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency below 1 MS
entries.summary: Uber redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while maintaining a cache hit rate above 99.9% and p99 disk-backed cache miss latency below 100 microseconds. The hybrid architecture combines in-memory keys and frequently accessed values with disk-backed storage, reducing garbage-collection overhead and memory consumption. By Leela Kumili
entries.content:
Uber has redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while keeping p99 cache miss latency below one millisecond. The hybrid architecture retains translation keys and frequently accessed values in memory while storing the remaining values on disk. The system serves millions of translations per second and maintains a cache hit rate above 99.9%.

The optimization addresses two problems identified through memory profiling across Uber's Go services. Garbage collection (GC) consumed more than 20% of CPU utilization in some services, with translations accounting for approximately 70% of allocated objects.

Uber Engineering noted that:

At Uber's scale, even small inefficiencies in memory management can add up.

The first optimization replaced Go's sync.Map with a conventional map[string]string protected by an RWMutex. The workload was predominantly read-heavy, with infrequent updates and no individual deletions. The previous implementation created multiple objects and pointers for each translation entry, increasing GC overhead. Moving to a value-based map reduced object allocations and improved CPU utilization by more than 30% in the affected service.

However, reducing object allocations did not solve the overall memory consumption problem. Translation datasets could contain two to three million keys, although individual services typically accessed only a small subset. Cache refreshes introduced another issue: the service built a replacement cache in the background before atomically swapping it with the existing one. Both copies therefore occupied memory simultaneously, causing some services to run out of memory during refreshes.

Uber considered external caching and generating service-specific translation subsets, but both introduced additional operational or maintenance costs. The team instead adopted a hybrid storage design that preserves the existing Get() and Put() API. All keys remain available in memory for fast lookups, while translation values are stored in disk-backed files.

Uber's hybrid translation cache (Source: Uber Blog Post)

The implementation uses 256 shards, each with its own read-write mutex, in-memory entries, and disk file. Six-byte hash-based keys reduce metadata overhead, with a fallback to the original key format to handle collisions. A time-based global least recently used (LRU) policy manages in-memory entries. During cache refreshes, the system uses access history to preload translations accessed within the previous 15 minutes, avoiding a cold cache after the swap.

In one example, a translation dataset that previously consumed approximately 800 MB in memory required around 40 MB for metadata after the redesign. With a configured limit of 50,000 in-memory entries, actual memory consumption typically ranged between 80 MB and 120 MB. In another reported workload, approximately 30,000 of more than four million entries were loaded in memory, while the cache hit rate remained above 99.9%. The p99 latency for disk-backed cache misses stayed below 100 microseconds.

Memory usage decreased from approximately 2.7 GB to 750 MB (Source: Uber Blog Post)

Uber's experience highlights the cost implications of in-memory caching at scale. The team recommends minimizing object references to reduce GC overhead and measuring how frequently cached values are accessed. When only a small proportion of cached data is actively used, a hybrid approach can retain frequently accessed values in memory while moving the rest to disk.
